newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian industry ask for lower interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Indian industry ask for lower interest rates.

text.p: India will soon have to lower interest rates and increase liquidity to help industrial output and prevent a feared economic slowdown, analysts said on Sunday.
They said industry, traders and the stock markets were eagerly looking to the government to help the economy break out of what they called a mid-year lull.
India's overall industry growth was a provisional 9.9 percent during April/June, against 15.5 percent in the same period last year.

Many Indian firms and exporters have complained that the shortage of liquidity, high interest rates and increasing boottlenecks in the country's creaking infrastructure are the main reasons behind the slowdown.

"The decline in industry was expected as there is a credit shortage, high interest rates and infrastructural bottlenecks," S.P. Gupta, director of the Indian Council of Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER) said.
"The government has to make its intention known. Until now, the expectations are for an easy credit policy to boost liquidity in the market," Gupta said.

Despite an average annual inflation rate of around five percent in the past six months, the prime lending rates of banks and financial institutions have remained between 16 and 17 percent, among the highest in the world.
The shortage of funds has forced many companies to hold back on fresh investment and expansion plans, which is crucial in generating a higher level of economic activity and growth.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram told Reuters Financial Television on Friday in New York that banks should cut their interest rates.

The central bank is expected to announce its latest credit policy this month, which is seen setting the agenda for industry and trade in the coming months of the current fiscal year ending on March 31, 1997.
The Reserve Bank of India expects interest rates to be lowered in the coming months. This would lower the cost of money, spur investment and industrial growth.
"The government has to create conditions to improve liquidity in the stock market and loosen rules to lure back retail investors," stock broker Ramesh Damani said.
"I cannot see any fundamental weakness in the economy, yet the stock market remains sluggish," Chidambaram said. "The stock markets needs to reform themselves to woo small investors."

The Securities and Exchange Board of India is currently clearing around 150 applications from foreign institutional investors seeking permission to operate here. So far more than 300 of them have invested more than $5 billion in Indian stocks since they were allowed to do so in 1993.
Indian exporters have also persistently complained of a credit shortage to promote overseas sales.
"The availability of export finance and the lowering of interest rates is necessary to step up exports," said P.K. Rajgarhia, head of a north Indian chamber of commerce.

Commerce Minister Bola Bulli Ramaiah said on Friday that the central bank would soon unveil a plan to stimulate exports. These grew 2.38 percent year on year in August, far below the 20.66 percent year on year in August 1995.
